meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Have you two been dating for a long time?
And we are only dating starting today.
And we already saw what happened next.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('I') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: I won a lucky ticket.
No, I am not running away.
Do you feel bad with me right now?

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('not') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: No, I am not running away.
Chef, come on, do not keep us in suspense.

examples.text: Герман ни в чём не виноват.
examples.trans: German is not to blame for anything.

дождаться.gloss: to wait for, to live to see

meanings.en: to wait for, to live to see
meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (root 'ждаться'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to wait for', forming an aspectual pair with 'дожидаться'.

examples.text: А Дмитрий Владимирович меня не дождался?
examples.trans: Did Dmitry Vladimirovich not wait for me?
I will wait for an answer.

examples.text: Я всё равно дождусь твоего ответа!
examples.trans: I will wait for your answer anyway!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (root 'казать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to say', forming an aspectual pair with 'говорить'.

examples.trans: I told you to work quickly!

examples.text: Скажите, он на меня очень злился?
examples.trans: Tell me, was he very angry with me?
What did you say?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('he') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Stop it, I know him well.
He used to work in Riga.
Give me the phone, I will call him.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.text: Виктория Сергеевна, можно тебя на минуту?
examples.trans: Viktoriya Sergeyevna, may I have a minute with you?
Dima, let's step aside for a minute.

examples.text: Иди лучше спокойно работай на кухне.
examples.trans: Better go work quietly in the kitchen.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.

examples.trans: I feel very good with you.
Well, there is a very long story there.
We have been friends for a very long time.

злиться.gloss: to be angry, to get mad

meanings.en: to be angry, to get mad
meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to be angry', forming an aspectual pair with 'разозлиться'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Скажите, он на меня очень злился?
examples.trans: Tell me, was he very angry with me?

examples.text: А знаешь, почему ты так злишься?
examples.trans: And do you know why you are so angry?
Don't be angry with me, please.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Good morning to all of you.
Have you two been dating for a long time?

examples.text: Виктория Сергеевна, у вас какие-то проблемы?
examples.trans: Viktoriya Sergeyevna, are you having some problems?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'too'.

examples.trans: And I want to help too.

examples.text: Виктория Сергеевна, вас тоже сюда вызвали?
examples.trans: Viktoriya Sergeyevna, did they summon you here too?
Me too.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'here'.

examples.trans: Come here, you little buddy of mine.

examples.text: Виктория Сергеевна, вас тоже сюда вызвали?
examples.trans: Viktoriya Sergeyevna, did they summon you here too?

examples.text: Или я сейчас зря сюда приехала?
examples.trans: Or did I come here in vain right now?

meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (root 'звать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to call', forming an aspectual pair with 'вызывать'.

examples.text: Виктория Сергеевна, вас тоже сюда вызвали?
examples.trans: Viktoriya Sergeyevna, did they summon you here too?
You called a sober driver!
We immediately called an ambulance.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('no') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: No, I am not running away.

examples.text: Говори, у меня от коллег нет секретов.
examples.trans: Speak, I have no secrets from colleagues.

examples.text: Нет его там в нашем списке.
examples.trans: He is not there on our list.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'just'.

examples.trans: Everything is just happening so fast.
He is just a total psycho!
Katyusha, I beg you, just calm down.

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (root 'ехать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to arrive', forming an aspectual pair with 'приезжать'.

examples.text: Только я приехала сегодня совсем ненадолго.
examples.trans: Only I came for just a short while tonight.

examples.text: Нет, я просто приехала вас поддержать.
examples.trans: No, I just came to support you.

examples.text: Или я сейчас зря сюда приехала?
examples.trans: Or did I come here in vain right now?

meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (root 'держать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to support', forming an aspectual pair with 'поддерживать'.

examples.text: Нет, я просто приехала вас поддержать.
examples.trans: No, I just came to support you.
If you support me, we will break through.
The friends decided to support Samson.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to want', forming an aspectual pair with 'захотеть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: I wanted to lift your spirits.

examples.text: Я же просто хотел тебе помочь.
examples.trans: I just wanted to help you.
Do you want some? It is very healthy.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'so that', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Не хотела, чтобы ваш вечер испортился.
examples.trans: I did not want your evening to be ruined.
So that there are witnesses.
I'm calling to say thank you.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('your') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.text: А вот это разве не ваш нож?
examples.trans: Isn't this one right here your knife?

examples.text: Шеф, расскажите, пожалуйста, весь ваш план.
examples.trans: Chef, please tell us your whole plan.

examples.text: Не хотела, чтобы ваш вечер испортился.
examples.trans: I did not want your evening to be ruined.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'evening', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Но у меня планы на вечер.
examples.trans: But I have plans for the evening.
We will meet in the evening after work.

examples.text: Не хотела, чтобы ваш вечер испортился.
examples.trans: I did not want your evening to be ruined.

meanings.note: Prefix 'ис-' ('out from within') marks extraction or exhaustion (root 'портиться'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to spoil'.

examples.text: Не хотела, чтобы ваш вечер испортился.
examples.trans: I did not want your evening to be ruined.
I thought that the groceries had spoiled.
I thought that they had spoiled.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'or', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Are you a real man or what?

examples.text: Или я сейчас зря сюда приехала?
examples.trans: Or did I come here in vain right now?

examples.text: Или ты тихо уходишь из ресторана.
examples.trans: Either you quietly leave the restaurant.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'now'.

examples.trans: Do you feel bad with me right now?
We have a lot of work right now.
I will slice everything up quickly right now.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'for nothing'.

examples.text: Или я сейчас зря сюда приехала?
examples.trans: Or did I come here in vain right now?
You're wasting your time.
I came for nothing.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('yes') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Yes, Katyusha, eat up, eat.
Yes, we are taking a very big risk.

examples.text: Да ты в чёрном списке посмотри.
examples.trans: Just look at the blacklist.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('well') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Well, there is a very long story there.
Chef, come on, do not keep us in suspense.
Vitya, just accept it already.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Senya, why are you embarrassing people?

examples.text: Это что, наш Герман, что ли?
examples.trans: Wait, is that our German or what?

examples.text: А что с ним дальше было?
examples.trans: And what happened to him after that?

говорить.gloss: to speak, to say, to talk

meanings.en: to speak, to say, to talk
meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to speak', forming an aspectual pair with 'сказать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: Vitya, why are you talking like that?

examples.text: Говори, у меня от коллег нет секретов.
examples.trans: Speak, I have no secrets from colleagues.
I am talking about your German.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'for' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: Thank you very much for the information.
German courted a waitress for a long time.

examples.text: Надо узнать, что это за таблетки.
examples.trans: We need to find out what kind of pills these are.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('this') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.text: Это что, наш Герман, что ли?
examples.trans: Wait, is that our German or what?
I wonder where all this took place?
That is my acquaintance Markus.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'grateful', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.text: Я вам за это очень благодарен.
examples.trans: I am very grateful to you for this.
I am very grateful to you.

examples.text: Я получил урок. Я благодарен Ивану Васильевичу за честное мнение.
examples.trans: I learned a lesson. I am grateful to Ivan Vasilyevich for his honest opinion.

meanings.note: Prefix 'на-' marks surface contact, accumulation, or completing a quantity (root 'деяться'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to hope', forming an aspectual pair with 'понадеяться'.

examples.text: Надеюсь, нам больше ничего не помешает.
examples.trans: I hope nothing else will get in our way.
I hope you understood me.
I hope so. Go on, act quickly!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('we') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Hey there, who do we have here?
We have been friends for a very long time.
And we are only dating starting today.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'a lot'.

examples.trans: We have a lot of work right now.
We've done a lot.
Too much to do.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('nothing') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.text: Ничего страшного, я сама всё приготовлю.
examples.trans: It is nothing serious, I will prepare everything myself.

examples.text: Смотри только ничего там не перепутай.
examples.trans: Just make sure you do not mix anything up there.

examples.text: Надеюсь, нам больше ничего не помешает.
examples.trans: I hope nothing else will get in our way.

помешать.gloss: to disturb, to interrupt; to hinder

meanings.en: to disturb, to interrupt; to hinder
meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (root 'мешать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to disturb', forming an aspectual pair with 'мешать'.

examples.text: Надеюсь, нам больше ничего не помешает.
examples.trans: I hope nothing else will get in our way.
Am I interrupting?
I won't disturb you.

meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (root 'ождать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to wait', forming an aspectual pair with 'ждать'.

examples.text: Подожди, что значит это слово опять?
examples.trans: Wait, what does that word 'again' mean?

examples.text: Подождите меня одну минуту в кабинете.
examples.trans: Wait for me for one minute in the office.
Wait, I'll be right there.

meanings.note: Everyday conversational Russian num meaning 'one', frequent in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Look, there is one more video clip.
Give me just one.
I have one brother.

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'minute', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Виктория Сергеевна, можно тебя на минуту?
examples.trans: Viktoriya Sergeyevna, may I have a minute with you?
Dima, let's step aside for a minute.

examples.text: Подождите меня одну минуту в кабинете.
examples.trans: Wait for me for one minute in the office.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: He used to work in Riga.
It happened in Riga.
And in the end she agreed.

meanings.note: From French 'cabinet' (private study or office).

examples.text: Я не знаю, они у него в кабинете.
examples.trans: I do not know, he keeps them in his office.

examples.text: Подождите меня одну минуту в кабинете.
examples.trans: Wait for me for one minute in the office.

examples.text: Витя, я уже вышла из кабинета.
examples.trans: Vitya, I have already stepped out of the office.

meanings.note: Everyday conversational Russian interj meaning 'hello', frequent in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello, Markus, hi there, my friend.

examples.text: Алло, да, конечно, я скоро буду.
examples.trans: Hello, yes, of course, I will be there soon.

examples.text: Алло, да, Витя, я уже вышла.
examples.trans: Hello, yes, Vitya, I have already stepped out.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'already'.

examples.trans: Have you two been dating for a long time?
We have been friends for a very long time.
And we already saw what happened next.

выйти.gloss: to go out, to get out

meanings.en: to go out, to get out
meanings.note: Russian perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to go out', forming an aspectual pair with 'выходить'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Алло, да, Витя, я уже вышла.
examples.trans: Hello, yes, Vitya, I have already stepped out.

examples.text: Витя, я уже вышла из кабинета.
examples.trans: Vitya, I have already stepped out of the office.

examples.text: Я выйду отсюда через две недели.
examples.trans: I'll be out of here in two weeks.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'from' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: They ordered a horsemeat steak out there.

examples.text: Его так легко вывести из себя?
